relationships.relationship: Le Goff credits Bloch’s combination of intellectual structure and medieval erudition as a resource for his formation and later endorses his analysis of complex social arrangements.
relationships.evidence_note: Le Goff’s own retrospective testimony establishes a specific intellectual debt, not personal teaching. The later methodological endorsement is jointly authored with Jean-Claude Schmitt; it neither rejects all earlier scholarship nor certifies a complete reading of the cited Bloch works.

relationships.relationship: Le Goff identifies Braudel’s placing geographical space at the center of historical inquiry as an inspiring resource during his formation.
relationships.evidence_note: Primary retrospective testimony, not an inference from institutional succession. It concerns the spatial approach exemplified by La Méditerranée; it does not claim Le Goff adopted every Braudelian thesis.

relationships.relationship: Le Goff invokes Febvre’s unconventional biographies as precedents when explaining his own Saint Louis project.
relationships.evidence_note: His retrospective account names Luther and Marguerite de Navarre despite Annales’ reputation for avoiding biography. This bounded methodological precedent is not a claim of personal mentorship.

relationships.relationship: Nora’s invitation to introduce O’Connell’s collection brought Le Goff to Saint Louis’s reported words, an encounter he identifies in explaining the origin of his biographical project.
relationships.evidence_note: Le Goff’s own opening account credits an editorial invitation and the resulting source encounter. O’Connell compiled the texts; Nora did not write them or supply the whole biography’s method. The retrospective approximate project date is not a precisely dated commission.

relationships.relationship: Le Goff questions Duby’s exaggerated instrumentalization and silence of medieval women while praising his recovery of their historical presence.
relationships.evidence_note: In his own answers to Klapisch-Zuber, Le Goff balances criticism with praise. Her questions are not automatically attributed to him; no inferred personal motives or wholesale rejection of Duby is asserted.

relationships.relationship: Davis praises The Birth of Purgatory but asks for more rigorous causal links between its cultural parallels, especially cartography and judicial practice (1985).
relationships.evidence_note: Her signed review accepts converging evidence for some arguments while distinguishing asserted affinities from demonstrated connections. It questions the birth metaphor without rejecting the book’s achievement. Review of Goldhammer’s 1984 translation; monograph unread.

relationships.relationship: While accepting Le Goff’s medieval cultural turning point, Ariès argues that his focus on purgatory as a place understates enduring older beliefs in repose and waiting (1983).
relationships.evidence_note: Printed pp. 153–156. Ariès accepts the terminus ad quem and cultural significance. His diffusion discussion allows regional variation and revises his own earlier late dating; this is no blanket denial of Le Goff’s thesis. French book (1981) not independently read.

relationships.relationship: Reviewing Moreira, Brown rejects the doctrinal-stagnation framing exemplified by Le Goff’s chapter heading and endorses continuing creative theological debate in the early Middle Ages (2012).
relationships.evidence_note: Brown names Le Goff, then states his own counterclaim in the Moreira discussion. Moreira’s contribution and her criticism of Brown’s earlier Irish-law explanation remain explicit. This is a scoped critical reception, not Brown’s independent refutation of every claim in the unread book.

relationships.relationship: Brown explicitly acknowledges Le Goff’s work among the studies that opened the field for his current research on death and the afterlife (1997).
relationships.evidence_note: Primary p. 1249 and n. 6. A bounded acknowledgment shared with other named scholars, not the derivation of Brown’s entire late-antique project. This earlier resource and his later criticism are distinct claims; the 1997 essay is not relabeled a direct personal attack.

relationships.relationship: Le Goff criticizes a tendency toward immobility in Braudelian history while retaining and extending its analysis of historical rhythms.
relationships.evidence_note: Le Goff’s own answer in the December 1988 interview, published in Spanish in 1991, criticizes a partial neglect of change. He expressly says neither Braudel nor Le Roy Ladurie actually wrote a truly immobile history, then describes a generalization of Braudel’s rhythms. This qualified criticism does not cancel the separately documented positive spatial debt. Braudel’s 1958 essay is discussed here through Le Goff’s testimony, not newly read.

relationships.relationship: Le Goff names Duby’s book on Bouvines as an exemplary way to write renewed event history.
relationships.evidence_note: In his own answer, Le Goff calls this a repeatedly cited successful example while discussing how to renew political and event history. This records a specific praised methodological model, not a comprehensive formative debt or an endorsement of all Duby’s arguments. Duby’s book was not newly read. This differs from Le Goff’s separate qualified criticism of Duby’s presentation of women.

relationships.relationship: Le Goff explicitly credits Chartier, alongside Jacques Revel, with collaboration essential to the original La Nouvelle Histoire project of 1978.
relationships.evidence_note: Le Goff’s 1988 acknowledgments and opening preface credit both collaborators. This is a contribution to a specified joint editorial project, not intellectual descent or sole authorship by Chartier. The 1988 abridged, updated collection is distinguished from the 1978 encyclopedia. Only the selected primary frontmatter transcription was read; the complete book and individual contributors’ essays were not newly read.

relationships.relationship: Schmitt attributes Le Goff’s reorientation toward medieval historical anthropology partly to the expanding influence of Lévi-Strauss’s structural anthropology.
relationships.evidence_note: This is explicitly Jean-Claude Schmitt’s named account reproduced by EPHE. It concerns the reorientation of Le Goff’s direction of studies, with other anthropologists also credited; it does not establish personal mentorship, a joint project, exclusive influence or wholesale adoption of structuralism. The passage is not Le Goff’s own acknowledgment. The Clio interview’s distinct Lévi-Strauss passage concerns Duby and is not used to infer this relationship.

relationships.relationship: Le Goff explicitly uses Goody’s Bagre research to explain oral remembering as narrative reconstruction rather than mechanical verbatim repetition.
relationships.evidence_note: Sustained named use in Memória, printed 429–430, alongside 427–428. This credits a specific analytical resource; it does not endorse a universal oral/written divide or establish every claim about LoDagaa culture. Goody’s underlying 1977 article is not independently read.

relationships.relationship: Le Goff draws on Yates’s account of artificial memory and its Renaissance transformations, including her interpretations of memory theatres and Bruno.
relationships.evidence_note: Sustained attributed use and explicit praise, printed 458–460. Yates’s reconstructions remain her interpretations as used by Le Goff; neither their universal acceptance nor her entire hermetic account is asserted. The cited 1966 book is not newly read.

relationships.relationship: Le Goff treats collective memory as both a historical resource and an object of power, calling for historical inquiry that broadens access to social remembering.
relationships.evidence_note: Complete Memória conclusion, printed 475–478. This records his specific program, not sole foundation of memory studies; it preserves the difference between historical inquiry and collective memory.

preservation: All earlier nodes, people, edges, biography and chronology exact; one old source verification receives an append-only reading note. No new life data/corpus counts. All78 reading files and archive unchanged.
